nodes.name: Reduce to submatrices
nodes.statement: We prove that $A'$ is TU by Definition~\ref{Matrix.IsTotallyUnimodular}. To this end, let $T'$ be a square submatrix of $A'$. Our goal is to show that $\det T' \in \{0, \pm 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing every square submatrix T' has determinant in {0,±1}.

nodes.name: Zero-row case
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be the submatrix of $A$ that represents $T'$ before pivoting. If some of the rows of $T$ were multiplied by zeros, then $T'$ contains zero rows, and hence $\det T' = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Case: a row was multiplied by zero, so det T' = 0.

nodes.name: Sign-flip case
nodes.statement: Otherwise, $T'$ was obtained from $T$ by multiplying certain rows by $-1$. Since $T'$ has finitely many rows, the number of such multiplications is also finite. Since multiplying a row by $-1$ results in the determinant getting multiplied by $-1$, we get $\det T' = \pm \det T \in \{0, \pm 1\}$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Case: only sign flips, so det T' = ±det T.

nodes.name: Define A''
nodes.statement: Let $X = \{1, \dots, k\} \setminus \{x\}$ and $Y = \{1, \dots, k\} \setminus \{y\}$, and let $A'' = A' (X, Y)$. Since $A''$ does not contain the pivot row or the pivot column, $\forall (i, j) \in X \times Y$ we have $A'' (i, j) = A (i, j) - \frac{A (i, y) \cdot A (x, j)}{A (x, y)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define A'' as the pivot result with pivot row and column removed and give its entries.

nodes.name: Cofactor expansion
nodes.statement: For $\forall j \in Y$, let $B_{j}$ be the matrix obtained from $A$ by removing row $x$ and column $j$, and let $B_{j}''$ be the matrix obtained from $A''$ by replacing column $j$ with $A (X, y)$ (i.e., the pivot column without the pivot element). The cofactor expansion along row $x$ in $A$ yields \[ \det A = \sum_{j = 1}^{k} (-1)^{y + j} \cdot A (x, j) \cdot \det B_{j}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Cofactor expansion of det A along the pivot row.

nodes.name: Reorder columns
nodes.statement: By reordering columns of every $B_{j}$ to match their order in $B_{j}''$, we get \[ \det A = (-1)^{x + y} \cdot \left( A (x, y) \cdot \det A' - \sum_{j \in Y} A (x, j) \cdot \det B_{j}'' \right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the expansion via the matrices B_j''.

nodes.name: Linearity
nodes.statement: By linearity of the determinant applied to $\det A''$, we have \[ \det A'' = \det A' - \sum_{j \in Y} \frac{A (x, j)}{A (x, y)} \cdot \det B_{j}'' \]
nodes.statement_short: Expand det A'' by multilinearity.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore, $|\det A''| = |\det A| / |A (x, y)|$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare the two expressions.

nodes.name: Regular implies TU signing
nodes.statement: Suppose that $M$ is regular. By Definition~\ref{Matroid.IsRegular}, there exists a TU matrix $A \in \mathbb{Q}^{X \times Y}$ such that $M$ is a vector matroid of $A$. By Lemma~\ref{StandardRepr.toMatroid_isBase_X}, $X$ (the row set of $B$) is a base of $M$. By Lemma~\ref{VectorMatroid.exists_standardRepr_isBase_isTotallyUnimodular}, $A$ can be converted into a standard representation matrix $B' \in \mathbb{Q}^{X \times Y}$ of $M$ such that $B'$ is also TU. Since $B'$ and $B$ are both standard representations of $M$, by Lemma~\ref{support_eq_support_of_same_matroid_same_X} the support matrices $(B')^{\#}$ and $B^{\#}$ are the same. Lemma \ref{Matrix.support_Z2} gives $B^{\#} = B$. Thus, $B'$ is TU and $(B')^{\#} = B$, so $B'$ is a TU signing of $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Only if: build a TU standard representation with the same support as B.

nodes.name: Unfold regularity
nodes.statement: Suppose that $M$ is regular. By Definition~\ref{Matroid.IsRegular}, there exists a TU matrix $A \in \mathbb{Q}^{X \times Y}$ such that $M$ is a vector matroid of $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Unfold regularity to get a TU representation A.

nodes.name: X is a base
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{StandardRepr.toMatroid_isBase_X}, $X$ (the row set of $B$) is a base of $M$.
nodes.statement_short: X is a base of M.

nodes.name: TU standard representation
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{VectorMatroid.exists_standardRepr_isBase_isTotallyUnimodular}, $A$ can be converted into a standard representation matrix $B' \in \mathbb{Q}^{X \times Y}$ of $M$ such that $B'$ is also TU.
nodes.statement_short: Convert A to a TU standard representation B'.

nodes.name: Same support
nodes.statement: Since $B'$ and $B$ are both standard representations of $M$, by Lemma~\ref{support_eq_support_of_same_matroid_same_X} the support matrices $(B')^{\#}$ and $B^{\#}$ are the same. Lemma \ref{Matrix.support_Z2} gives $B^{\#} = B$.
nodes.statement_short: B' and B have the same support, which equals B.

nodes.name: Conclude direction
nodes.statement: Thus, $B'$ is TU and $(B')^{\#} = B$, so $B'$ is a TU signing of $B$.
nodes.statement_short: B' is a TU signing of B.

nodes.name: TU signing implies regular
nodes.statement: Suppose that $B$ has a TU signing $B' \in \mathbb{Q}^{X \times Y}$. Then $A = [1 \mid B']$ is TU, as it is obtained from $B'$ by adjoining the identity matrix. Moreover, by Lemma~\ref{Matrix.IsTotallyUnimodular.toMatroid_eq_support_toMatroid}, $A$ represents the same matroid as $A^{\#} = [1 \mid B]$, which is $M$. Thus, $A$ is a TU matrix representing $M$, so $M$ is regular.
nodes.statement_short: If: [1|B'] is TU and represents M.

nodes.name: Adjoin identity
nodes.statement: Suppose that $B$ has a TU signing $B' \in \mathbb{Q}^{X \times Y}$. Then $A = [1 \mid B']$ is TU, as it is obtained from $B'$ by adjoining the identity matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Adjoin the identity to the signing to get a TU matrix A.

nodes.name: Same matroid
nodes.statement: Moreover, by Lemma~\ref{Matrix.IsTotallyUnimodular.toMatroid_eq_support_toMatroid}, $A$ represents the same matroid as $A^{\#} = [1 \mid B]$, which is $M$.
nodes.statement_short: A and its support represent the same matroid M.

nodes.name: Conclude direction
nodes.statement: Thus, $A$ is a TU matrix representing $M$, so $M$ is regular.
nodes.statement_short: M is regular.

nodes.name: Reduce to submatrices
nodes.statement: We prove that $B$ is TU by Definition~\ref{Matrix.IsTotallyUnimodular}. To this end, let $T$ be a square submatrix of $B$. Our goal is to show that $\det T \in \{0, \pm 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to square submatrices T of B.

nodes.name: Block form of T
nodes.statement: Let $T_{\ell}$ and $T_{r}$ denote the submatrices in the intersection of $T$ with $B_{\ell}$ and $B_{r}$, respectively. Then $T$ has the form \[ T = \begin{bmatrix} T_{\ell} & 0 \\ 0 & T_{r} \end{bmatrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: T is block diagonal with blocks T_l, T_r.

nodes.name: Square blocks
nodes.statement: First, suppose that $T_{\ell}$ and $T_{r}$ are square. Then $\det T = \det T_{\ell} \cdot \det T_{r}$ by Lemma~\ref{Matrix.det_fromBlocks_zero}. Moreover, $\det T_{\ell}, \det T_{r} \in \{0, \pm 1\}$, since $T_{\ell}$ and $T_{r}$ are square submatrices of TU matrices $B_{\ell}$ and $B_{r}$, respectively. Thus, $\det T \in \{0, \pm 1\}$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Square blocks: det T is a product of 0/±1 determinants.

nodes.name: Non-square blocks
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality we may assume that $T_{\ell}$ has fewer rows than columns. Otherwise we can transpose all matrices and use the same proof, since TUness and determinants are preserved under transposition. Thus, $T$ can be represented in the form \[ T = \begin{bmatrix} T_{11} & T_{12} \\ 0 & T_{22} \end{bmatrix}, \] where $T_{11}$ contains $T_{\ell}$ and some zero rows, $T_{22}$ is a submatrix of $T_{r}$, and $T_{12}$ contains the rest of the rows of $T_{r}$ (not contained in $T_{22}$) and some zero rows. By Lemma~\ref{Matrix.det_fromBlocks_zero}, we have $\det T = \det T_{11} \cdot \det T_{22}$. Since $T_{11}$ contains at least one zero row, $\det T_{11} = 0$. Thus, $\det T = 0 \in \{0, \pm 1\}$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Non-square blocks: a zero row forces det T = 0.

nodes.name: TU signings of summands
nodes.statement: Let $B_{\ell}$, $B_{r}$, and $B$ be standard $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ representation matrices from Definition~\ref{Matroid.IsSum1of}. Since $M_{\ell}$ and $M_{r}$ are regular, by Lemma~\ref{StandardRepr.toMatroid_isRegular_iff_hasTuSigning}, $B_{\ell}$ and $B_{r}$ have TU signings $B_{\ell}'$ and $B_{r}'$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Take standard representations and TU signings of the summands.

nodes.name: Sum of signings
nodes.statement: Then $B' = B_{\ell}' \oplus_{1} B_{r}'$ is a TU signing of $B$. Indeed, $B'$ is TU by Lemma~\ref{Matrix.fromBlocks_isTotallyUnimodular}, and a direct calculation shows that $B'$ is a signing of $B$.
nodes.statement_short: The 1-sum of the signings is a TU signing of B.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus, $M$ is regular by Lemma~\ref{StandardRepr.toMatroid_isRegular_iff_hasTuSigning}.
nodes.statement_short: M is regular by the signing criterion.

nodes.name: TU signings of summands
nodes.statement: Let $B_{\ell}$, $B_{r}$, and $B$ be standard $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ representation matrices from Definition~\ref{Matroid.IsSum2of}. Since $M_{\ell}$ and $M_{r}$ are regular, by Lemma~\ref{StandardRepr.toMatroid_isRegular_iff_hasTuSigning}, $B_{\ell}$ and $B_{r}$ have TU signings $B_{\ell}'$ and $B_{r}'$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Take standard representations and TU signings of the summands.

nodes.name: Sum of signings
nodes.statement: Then $B' = B_{\ell}' \oplus_{2, x, y} B_{r}'$ is a TU signing of $B$. Indeed, $B'$ is TU by Lemma~\ref{standardReprSum2_isTotallyUnimodular}, and a direct calculation verifies that $B'$ is a signing of $B$.
nodes.statement_short: The 2-sum of the signings is a TU signing of B.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus, $M$ is regular by Lemma~\ref{StandardRepr.toMatroid_isRegular_iff_hasTuSigning}.
nodes.statement_short: M is regular by the signing criterion.

nodes.name: TU signings of summands
nodes.statement: Let $B_{\ell}$, $B_{r}$, and $B$ be standard $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ representation matrices from Definition~\ref{Matroid.IsSum3of}. Since $M_{\ell}$ and $M_{r}$ are regular, by Lemma~\ref{StandardRepr.toMatroid_isRegular_iff_hasTuSigning}, $B_{\ell}$ and $B_{r}$ have TU signings.
nodes.statement_short: Summands have TU signings.

nodes.name: Canonical signing
nodes.statement: Then the canonical signing $B''$ from Definition~\ref{MatrixSum3.toCanonicalSigning} is a TU signing of $B$. Indeed, $B''$ is a signing of $B$ by Lemma~\ref{MatrixSum3.HasCanonicalSigning.toCanonicalSigning}, and $B''$ is TU by Lemma~\ref{MatrixSum3.IsCanonicalSigning.isTotallyUnimodular}.
nodes.statement_short: The canonical signing B'' is a TU signing of B.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus, $M$ is regular by Lemma~\ref{StandardRepr.toMatroid_isRegular_iff_hasTuSigning}.
nodes.statement_short: M is regular by the signing criterion.

nodes.name: Entries of r
nodes.statement: Since $B_{\ell}$ is TU, all its entries are in $\{0, \pm 1\}$. In particular, $r$ is a $\{0, \pm 1\}$ vector.
nodes.statement_short: r has entries in {0,±1}.

nodes.name: Structure of C
nodes.statement: Therefore, every column of $D$ is a copy of $y$, $-y$, or the zero column. Thus, $C$ can be obtained from $B_{r}$ by adjoining zero columns, duplicating the $y$ column, and multiplying some columns by $-1$.
nodes.statement_short: C arises from B_r by adjoining zero columns, duplicating and negating columns.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since all these operations preserve TUess and since $B_{r}$ is TU, $C$ is also TU.
nodes.statement_short: These operations preserve TU.

nodes.name: Name blocks
nodes.statement: Let \[ B_{\ell}' = \begin{bmatrix} A_{\ell}' \\ r' \end{bmatrix}, \quad B' = \begin{bmatrix} B_{11}' & B_{12}' \\ B_{21}' & B_{22}' \end{bmatrix} \] where the blocks have the same dimensions as in $B_{\ell}$ and $B$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Name the blocks of B_l' and B'.

nodes.name: Apply zero-block lemma
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{Matrix.shortTableauPivot_zero}, $B_{11}' = A_{\ell}'$, $B_{12}' = 0$, and $B_{22}' = A_{r}$.
nodes.statement_short: Three blocks follow from the zero-block pivot lemma.

nodes.name: Bottom-left block
nodes.statement: Equality $B_{21}' = c \otimes r'$ can be verified via a direct calculation.
nodes.statement_short: Bottom-left block by direct calculation.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus, $B' = B_{\ell}' \oplus_{2, x, y} B_{r}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude B' is the 2-sum.

nodes.name: Reduce to k-PU
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{Matrix.isTotallyUnimodular_iff_forall_isPartiallyUnimodular}, it suffices to show that $B_{\ell} \oplus_{2, x, y} B_{r}$ is $k$-PU for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$. We prove this claim by induction on $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce TU to k-PU for all k; induct on k.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: The base case with $k = 1$ holds, since all entries of $B_{\ell} \oplus_{2, x, y} B_{r}$ are in $\{0, \pm 1\}$ by construction.
nodes.statement_short: Base case: entries are in {0,±1}.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Suppose that for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$ we know that for any TU matrices $B_{\ell}'$ and $B_{r}'$ (from Definition~\ref{standardReprSum2}) their $2$-sum $B_{\ell}' \oplus_{2, x, y} B_{r}'$ is $k$-PU. Now, given TU matrices $B_{\ell}$ and $B_{r}$ (from Definition~\ref{standardReprSum2}), our goal is to show that $B = B_{\ell} \oplus_{2, x, y} B_{r}$ is $(k + 1)$-PU, i.e., that every $(k + 1) \times (k + 1)$ submatrix $T$ of $B$ has $\det T \in \{0, \pm 1\}$. First, suppose that $T$ has no rows in $X_{\ell}$. Then $T$ is a submatrix of $\begin{bmatrix} D & A_{r} \end{bmatrix}$, which is TU by Lemma~\ref{Matrix.IsTotallyUnimodular.fromCols_outer}, so $\det T \in \{0, \pm 1\}$. Thus, we may assume that $T$ contains a row $x_{\ell} \in X_{\ell}$. Next, note that without loss of generality we may assume that there exists $y_{\ell} \in Y_{\ell}$ such that $T (x_{\ell}, y_{\ell}) \neq 0$. Indeed, if $T (x_{\ell}, y) = 0$ for all $y$, then $\det T = 0$ and we are done, and $T (x_{\ell}, y) = 0$ holds whenever $y \in Y_{r}$. Since $B$ is $1$-PU, all entries of $T$ are in $\{0, \pm 1\}$, and hence $T (x_{\ell}, y_{\ell}) \in \{\pm 1\}$. Thus, by Lemma~\ref{shortTableauPivot_submatrix_det_abs_eq_div}, performing a short tableau pivot in $T$ on $(x_{\ell}, y_{\ell})$ yields a matrix that contains a $k \times k$ submatrix $T''$ such that $|\det T| = |\det T''|$. Since $T$ is a submatrix of $B$, matrix $T''$ is a submatrix of the matrix $B'$ resulting from performing a short tableau pivot in $B$ on the same entry $(x_{\ell}, y_{\ell})$. By Lemma~\ref{standardReprSum2_shortTableauPivot}, we have $B' = B_{\ell}' \oplus_{2, x, y} B_{r}$ where $B_{\ell}'$ is the result of performing a short tableau pivot in $B_{\ell}$ on $(x_{\ell}, y_{\ell})$. Since $B_{\ell}$ is TU, by Lemma \ref{Matrix.IsTotallyUnimodular.shortTableauPivot}, $B_{\ell}'$ is also TU. Thus, by the inductive hypothesis applied to $T''$ and $B_{\ell}' \oplus_{2, x, y} B_{r}$, we have $\det T'' \in \{0, \pm 1\}$. Since $|\det T| = |\det T''|$, we conclude that $\det T \in \{0, \pm 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step via pivoting.

nodes.name: Inductive hypothesis
nodes.statement: Suppose that for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$ we know that for any TU matrices $B_{\ell}'$ and $B_{r}'$ (from Definition~\ref{standardReprSum2}) their $2$-sum $B_{\ell}' \oplus_{2, x, y} B_{r}'$ is $k$-PU. Now, given TU matrices $B_{\ell}$ and $B_{r}$ (from Definition~\ref{standardReprSum2}), our goal is to show that $B = B_{\ell} \oplus_{2, x, y} B_{r}$ is $(k + 1)$-PU, i.e., that every $(k + 1) \times (k + 1)$ submatrix $T$ of $B$ has $\det T \in \{0, \pm 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: State the inductive hypothesis and goal.

nodes.name: No rows in X_l
nodes.statement: First, suppose that $T$ has no rows in $X_{\ell}$. Then $T$ is a submatrix of $\begin{bmatrix} D & A_{r} \end{bmatrix}$, which is TU by Lemma~\ref{Matrix.IsTotallyUnimodular.fromCols_outer}, so $\det T \in \{0, \pm 1\}$. Thus, we may assume that $T$ contains a row $x_{\ell} \in X_{\ell}$.
nodes.statement_short: If T has no rows in X_l, it lies in the TU matrix [D A_r].

nodes.name: Nonzero pivot
nodes.statement: Next, note that without loss of generality we may assume that there exists $y_{\ell} \in Y_{\ell}$ such that $T (x_{\ell}, y_{\ell}) \neq 0$. Indeed, if $T (x_{\ell}, y) = 0$ for all $y$, then $\det T = 0$ and we are done, and $T (x_{\ell}, y) = 0$ holds whenever $y \in Y_{r}$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG a nonzero entry in row x_l within Y_l.

nodes.name: Pivot and apply hypothesis
nodes.statement: Since $B$ is $1$-PU, all entries of $T$ are in $\{0, \pm 1\}$, and hence $T (x_{\ell}, y_{\ell}) \in \{\pm 1\}$. Thus, by Lemma~\ref{shortTableauPivot_submatrix_det_abs_eq_div}, performing a short tableau pivot in $T$ on $(x_{\ell}, y_{\ell})$ yields a matrix that contains a $k \times k$ submatrix $T''$ such that $|\det T| = |\det T''|$. Since $T$ is a submatrix of $B$, matrix $T''$ is a submatrix of the matrix $B'$ resulting from performing a short tableau pivot in $B$ on the same entry $(x_{\ell}, y_{\ell})$. By Lemma~\ref{standardReprSum2_shortTableauPivot}, we have $B' = B_{\ell}' \oplus_{2, x, y} B_{r}$ where $B_{\ell}'$ is the result of performing a short tableau pivot in $B_{\ell}$ on $(x_{\ell}, y_{\ell})$. Since $B_{\ell}$ is TU, by Lemma \ref{Matrix.IsTotallyUnimodular.shortTableauPivot}, $B_{\ell}'$ is also TU. Thus, by the inductive hypothesis applied to $T''$ and $B_{\ell}' \oplus_{2, x, y} B_{r}$, we have $\det T'' \in \{0, \pm 1\}$. Since $|\det T| = |\det T''|$, we conclude that $\det T \in \{0, \pm 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pivot to a k x k submatrix of a 2-sum of TU matrices and apply the hypothesis.

nodes.name: Q' is a TU signing
nodes.statement: Since $Q$ is a TU signing of $S$ and $Q'$ is obtained from $Q$ by multiplying rows and columns by $\pm 1$ factors, $Q'$ is also a TU signing of $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Q' is still a TU signing of S.

nodes.name: Compute entries
nodes.statement_short: Compute seven entries of Q'.

nodes.name: Remaining entries
nodes.statement: Thus, it remains to show that $Q' (x_{0}, y_{1}) = S' (x_{0}, y_{1})$ and $Q' (x_{1}, y_{1}) = S' (x_{1}, y_{1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Two entries remain.

nodes.name: Entry (x0,y1)
nodes.statement: Consider the entry $Q' (x_{0}, y_{1})$. If $D_{0} (x_{0}, y_{1}) = 0$, then $Q' (x_{0}, y_{1}) = 0 = S' (x_{0}, y_{1})$. Otherwise, we have $D_{0} (x_{0}, y_{1}) = 1$, and so $Q' (x_{0}, y_{1}) \in \{\pm 1\}$, as $Q'$ is a signing of $S$. If $Q' (x_{0}, y_{1}) = -1$, then \[ \det Q' (\{x_{0}, x_{2}\}, \{y_{0}, y_{1}\}) = \det \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = 2 \notin \{0, \pm 1\}, \] which contradicts TUness of $Q'$. Thus, $Q' (x_{0}, y_{1}) = 1 = S' (x_{0}, y_{1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Entry (x_0,y_1) is forced by TUness.

nodes.name: Entry (x1,y1)
nodes.statement: Consider the entry $Q' (x_{1}, y_{1})$. Since $Q'$ is a signing of $S$, we have $Q' (x_{1}, y_{1}) \in \{\pm 1\}$. Consider two cases. \begin{enumerate} \item Suppose that $D_{0} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. If $Q' (x_{1}, y_{1}) = 1$, then $ \det Q = \det \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = -2 \notin \{0, \pm 1\}, $ which contradicts TUness of $Q'$. Thus, $Q' (x_{1}, y_{1}) = -1 = S' (x_{1}, y_{1})$. \item Suppose that $D_{0} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. If $Q' (x_{1}, y_{1}) = -1$, then $ \det Q (\{x_{1}, x_{0}\}, \{y_{1}, y_{2}\}) = \det \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = 2 \notin \{0, \pm 1\}, $ which contradicts TUness of $Q'$. Thus, $Q' (x_{1}, y_{1}) = 1 = S' (x_{1}, y_{1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Entry (x_1,y_1) is forced by TUness in each normal form of D_0.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Consider the entry $Q' (x_{1}, y_{1})$. Since $Q'$ is a signing of $S$, we have $Q' (x_{1}, y_{1}) \in \{\pm 1\}$. Consider two cases.
nodes.statement_short: The entry is ±1; split on D_0.

nodes.name: Identity case
nodes.statement: Suppose that $D_{0} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. If $Q' (x_{1}, y_{1}) = 1$, then $ \det Q = \det \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = -2 \notin \{0, \pm 1\}, $ which contradicts TUness of $Q'$. Thus, $Q' (x_{1}, y_{1}) = -1 = S' (x_{1}, y_{1})$.
nodes.statement_short: D_0 identity: entry must be -1.

nodes.name: Unitriangular case
nodes.statement: Suppose that $D_{0} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. If $Q' (x_{1}, y_{1}) = -1$, then $ \det Q (\{x_{1}, x_{0}\}, \{y_{1}, y_{2}\}) = \det \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = 2 \notin \{0, \pm 1\}, $ which contradicts TUness of $Q'$. Thus, $Q' (x_{1}, y_{1}) = 1 = S' (x_{1}, y_{1})$.
nodes.statement_short: D_0 unitriangular: entry must be 1.

nodes.name: Summands are signings
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{Matrix.HasTuCanonicalSigning.toCanonicalSigning}, $B_{\ell}''$ and $B_{r}''$ are TU signings of $B_{\ell}$ and $B_{r}$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Re-signed summands are TU signings.

nodes.name: Inherited blocks
nodes.statement: As a result, blocks $A_{\ell}''$, $A_{r}''$, $D_{\ell}''$, $D_{r}''$, and $D_{0}''$ in $B''$ are signings of the corresponding blocks in $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Inherited blocks are signings.

nodes.name: Bottom-left block
nodes.statement: Thus, it remains to show that $D_{\ell r}''$ is a signing of $D_{\ell r}$. This can be verified via a direct calculation.
nodes.statement_short: D_lr'' is a signing of D_lr by calculation.

nodes.name: B_r'' is TU
nodes.statement: Throughout the proof we use that $B_{r}''$ is TU, which holds by Lemma~\ref{Matrix.HasTuCanonicalSigning.toCanonicalSigning}.
nodes.statement_short: B_r'' is TU.

nodes.name: Item 1
nodes.statement: Since $B_{r}''$ is TU, all its entries are in $\{0, \pm 1\}$, and in particular $\begin{bmatrix} c_{0}'' (i) & c_{1}'' (i) \end{bmatrix} \in \{0, \pm 1\}^{\{y_{0}, y_{1}\}}$. If $\begin{bmatrix} c_{0}' (i) & c_{1}'' (i) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, then \[ \det B_{r}'' (\{x_{2}, i\}, \{y_{0}, y_{1}\}) = \det \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = -2 \notin \{0, \pm 1\}, \] which contradicts TUness of $B_{r}''$. Similarly, if $\begin{bmatrix} c_{0}'' (i) & c_{1}'' (i) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} $, then \[ \det B_{r}'' (\{x_{2}, i\}, \{y_{0}, y_{1}\}) = \det \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = 2 \notin \{0, \pm 1\}, \] which contradicts TUness of $B_{r}''$. Thus, the desired statement holds.
nodes.statement_short: Item 1: forbidden sign patterns give a 2x2 minor of absolute value 2.

nodes.name: Item 2
nodes.statement: Follows from item~\ref{item:tss_Brp_c01} and a direct calculation.
nodes.statement_short: Item 2 from item 1.

nodes.name: Item 3
nodes.statement: Performing a short tableau pivot in $B_{r}''$ on $(x_{2}, y_{0})$ yields: \[ B_{r}'' = \begin{bmatrix} \fbox{1} & 1 & 0 \\ c_{0} & c_{1} & A_{r} \end{bmatrix} \quad \to \quad \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -c_{0} & c_{1}'' - c_{0} & A_{r} \end{bmatrix} \] The resulting matrix can be transformed into $\begin{bmatrix} c_{0}'' & c_{2}'' & A_{r}'' \end{bmatrix}$ by removing row $x_{2}$ and multiplying columns $y_{0}$ and $y_{1}$ by $-1$. Since $B_{r}''$ is TU and since TUness is preserved under pivoting, taking submatrices, multiplying columns by ${\pm 1}$ factors, we conclude that $\begin{bmatrix} c_{0}'' & c_{2}'' & A_{r}'' \end{bmatrix}$ is TU.
nodes.statement_short: Item 3: pivot on (x_2,y_0) and use TU-preserving operations.

nodes.name: Item 4
nodes.statement: Similar to item~\ref{item:tss_Brp_tu2}, performing a short tableau pivot in $B_{r}''$ on $(x_{2}, y_{1})$ yields: \[ B_{r}'' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \fbox{1} & 0 \\ c_{0} & c_{1} & A_{r} \end{bmatrix} \quad \to \quad \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ c_{0}'' - c_{1} & -c_{1} & A_{r} \end{bmatrix} \] The resulting matrix can be transformed into $\begin{bmatrix} c_{1}'' & c_{2}'' & A_{r}'' \end{bmatrix}$ by removing row $x_{2}$, multiplying column $y_{1}$ by $-1$, and swapping the order of columns $y_{0}$ and $y_{1}$. Since $B_{r}''$ is TU and since TUness is preserved under pivoting, taking submatrices, multiplying columns by ${\pm 1}$ factors, and re-ordering columns, we conclude that $\begin{bmatrix} c_{1}'' & c_{2}'' & A_{r}'' \end{bmatrix}$ is TU.
nodes.statement_short: Item 4: pivot on (x_2,y_1).

nodes.name: Item 5
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a square submatrix of $\begin{bmatrix} c_{0}'' & c_{1}'' & c_{2}'' & A_{r}'' \end{bmatrix}$. Our goal is to show that $\det V \in \{0, \pm 1\}$. Suppose that column $c_{2}''$ is not in $V$. Then $V$ is a submatrix of $B_{r}''$, which is TU. Thus, $\det V \in \{0, \pm 1\}$. Going forward we assume that column $z$ is in $V$. Suppose that columns $c_{0}''$ and $c_{1}''$ are both in $V$. Then $V$ contains columns $c_{0}''$, $c_{1}''$, and $c_{2}'' = c_{0}'' - c_{1}''$, which are linearly. Thus, $\det V = 0$. Going forward we assume that at least one of the columns $c_{0}''$ and $c_{1}''$ is not in $V$. Suppose that column $c_{1}''$ is not in $V$. Then $V$ is a submatrix of $\begin{bmatrix} c_{0}'' & c_{2}'' & A_{r}'' \end{bmatrix}$, which is TU by item~\ref{item:tss_Brp_tu1}. Thus, $\det V \in \{0, \pm 1\}$. Similarly, if column $c_{0}''$ is not in $V$, then $V$ is a submatrix of $\begin{bmatrix} c_{1}'' & c_{2}'' & A_{r}'' \end{bmatrix}$, which is TU by item~\ref{item:tss_Brp_tu2}. Thus, $\det V \in \{0, \pm 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Item 5: case analysis on which of c_0'', c_1'', c_2'' are in V.

nodes.name: Fix V
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a square submatrix of $\begin{bmatrix} c_{0}'' & c_{1}'' & c_{2}'' & A_{r}'' \end{bmatrix}$. Our goal is to show that $\det V \in \{0, \pm 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a square submatrix V.

nodes.name: No c2
nodes.statement: Suppose that column $c_{2}''$ is not in $V$. Then $V$ is a submatrix of $B_{r}''$, which is TU. Thus, $\det V \in \{0, \pm 1\}$. Going forward we assume that column $z$ is in $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Without c_2'', V is a submatrix of B_r''.

nodes.name: All three columns
nodes.statement: Suppose that columns $c_{0}''$ and $c_{1}''$ are both in $V$. Then $V$ contains columns $c_{0}''$, $c_{1}''$, and $c_{2}'' = c_{0}'' - c_{1}''$, which are linearly. Thus, $\det V = 0$. Going forward we assume that at least one of the columns $c_{0}''$ and $c_{1}''$ is not in $V$.
nodes.statement_short: c_0'', c_1'', c_2'' together are dependent.

nodes.name: One of c0, c1 missing
nodes.statement: Suppose that column $c_{1}''$ is not in $V$. Then $V$ is a submatrix of $\begin{bmatrix} c_{0}'' & c_{2}'' & A_{r}'' \end{bmatrix}$, which is TU by item~\ref{item:tss_Brp_tu1}. Thus, $\det V \in \{0, \pm 1\}$. Similarly, if column $c_{0}''$ is not in $V$, then $V$ is a submatrix of $\begin{bmatrix} c_{1}'' & c_{2}'' & A_{r}'' \end{bmatrix}$, which is TU by item~\ref{item:tss_Brp_tu2}. Thus, $\det V \in \{0, \pm 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise use items 3 and 4.

nodes.name: Item 1
nodes.statement: Holds by Lemma~\ref{MatrixSum3.HasTuBr.cccAr_isTotallyUnimodular}.\ref{item:tss_Brp_c2}.
nodes.statement_short: Item 1 from Lemma 31.

nodes.name: Item 2
nodes.statement: Note that \[ \begin{bmatrix} D_{\ell}'' \\ D_{\ell r}'' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} D_{0}'' \\ D_{r}'' \end{bmatrix} \cdot (D_{0}'')^{-1} \cdot D_{\ell}'', \quad \begin{bmatrix} D_{0}'' \\ D_{r}'' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} D_{0}'' \\ D_{r}'' \end{bmatrix} \cdot (D_{0}'')^{-1} \cdot D_{0}'', \quad \begin{bmatrix} D_{0}'' \\ D_{r}'' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} c_{0}'' & c_{1}'' \end{bmatrix}, \quad \begin{bmatrix} D_{\ell}'' & D_{0}'' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} d_{0}'' \\ d_{1}'' \end{bmatrix}. \] Thus, \[ D'' = \begin{bmatrix} D_{\ell}'' & D_{0}'' \\ D_{\ell r}'' & D_{r}'' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} D_{0}'' \\ D_{r}'' \end{bmatrix} \cdot (D_{0}'')^{-1} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} D_{\ell}'' & D_{0}'' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} c_{0}'' & c_{1}'' \end{bmatrix} \cdot (D_{0}'')^{-1} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} d_{0}'' \\ d_{1}'' \end{bmatrix}. \] Considering the two cases for $D_{0}''$ and performing the calculations yields the desired results.
nodes.statement_short: Item 2: factor D'' through (D_0'')^{-1} and compute.

nodes.name: Item 3
nodes.statement: Let $j \in Y_{\ell}$. By Lemma~\ref{MatrixSum3.HasTuBr.dddAl_isTotallyUnimodular}.\ref{item:tss_Blp_d01}, $\begin{bmatrix} d_{0}'' (i) \\ d_{1}'' (j) \end{bmatrix} \in \{0, \pm 1\}^{\{x_{1}, x_{0}\}} \setminus \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \right\}$. Consider two cases. \begin{enumerate} \item If $D_{0}'' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, then by item~\ref{item:tss_Bp_Deq} we have $D'' (X_{r}, j) = d_{0}'' (j) \cdot c_{0}'' + (-d_{1}'' (j)) \cdot c_{1}''$. By considering all possible cases for $d_{0}'' (j)$ and $d_{1}'' (j)$, we conclude that $D'' (X_{r}, j) \in \{0, \pm c_{0}'', \pm c_{1}'', \pm (c_{0}'' - c_{1}'')\}$. \item If $D_{0}'' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, then by item~\ref{item:tss_Bp_Deq} we have $D'' (X_{r}, j) = (d_{0}'' (j) - d_{1}'' (j)) \cdot c_{0}'' + d_{1}'' (j) \cdot c_{1}''$. By considering all possible cases for $d_{0}'' (j)$ and $d_{1}'' (j)$, we conclude that $D'' (X_{r}, j) \in \{0, \pm c_{0}'', \pm c_{1}'', \pm (c_{0}'' - c_{1}'')\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Item 3: columns of D'' are 0 or ±c_i''.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Let $j \in Y_{\ell}$. By Lemma~\ref{MatrixSum3.HasTuBr.dddAl_isTotallyUnimodular}.\ref{item:tss_Blp_d01}, $\begin{bmatrix} d_{0}'' (i) \\ d_{1}'' (j) \end{bmatrix} \in \{0, \pm 1\}^{\{x_{1}, x_{0}\}} \setminus \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \right\}$. Consider two cases.
nodes.statement_short: Sign patterns of d_0'', d_1'' from Lemma 32.

nodes.name: Case 1
nodes.statement: If $D_{0}'' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, then by item~\ref{item:tss_Bp_Deq} we have $D'' (X_{r}, j) = d_{0}'' (j) \cdot c_{0}'' + (-d_{1}'' (j)) \cdot c_{1}''$. By considering all possible cases for $d_{0}'' (j)$ and $d_{1}'' (j)$, we conclude that $D'' (X_{r}, j) \in \{0, \pm c_{0}'', \pm c_{1}'', \pm (c_{0}'' - c_{1}'')\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Case D_0'' = diag(1,-1).

nodes.name: Case 2
nodes.statement: If $D_{0}'' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, then by item~\ref{item:tss_Bp_Deq} we have $D'' (X_{r}, j) = (d_{0}'' (j) - d_{1}'' (j)) \cdot c_{0}'' + d_{1}'' (j) \cdot c_{1}''$. By considering all possible cases for $d_{0}'' (j)$ and $d_{1}'' (j)$, we conclude that $D'' (X_{r}, j) \in \{0, \pm c_{0}'', \pm c_{1}'', \pm (c_{0}'' - c_{1}'')\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Case D_0'' unitriangular.

nodes.name: Item 4
nodes.statement: Let $i \in X_{r}$. By Lemma~\ref{MatrixSum3.HasTuBr.cccAr_isTotallyUnimodular}.\ref{item:tss_Brp_c01}, $\begin{bmatrix} c_{0}'' (i) & c_{1}'' (i) \end{bmatrix} \in \{0, \pm 1\}^{\{y_{0}, y_{1}\}} \setminus \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \right\}$. Consider two cases. \begin{enumerate} \item If $D_{0}'' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, then by item~\ref{item:tss_Bp_Deq} we have $D'' (i, Y_{\ell}) = c_{0}'' (i) \cdot d_{0}'' + (-c_{1}'' (i)) \cdot d_{1}''$. By considering all possible cases for $c_{0}'' (i)$ and $c_{1}'' (i)$, we conclude that $D'' (i, Y_{\ell}) \in \{0, \pm d_{0}'', \pm d_{1}'', \pm d_{2}''\}$. \item If $D_{0}'' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, then by item~\ref{item:tss_Bp_Deq} we have $D'' (i, Y_{\ell}) = c_{0}'' (i) \cdot d_{0}'' + (c_{1}'' (i) - c_{0}'' (i)) \cdot d_{1}''$. By considering all possible cases for $c_{0}'' (i)$ and $c_{1}'' (i)$, we conclude that $D'' (i, Y_{\ell}) \in \{0, \pm d_{0}'', \pm d_{1}'', \pm d_{2}''\}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Item 4: rows of D'' are 0 or ±d_i''.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Let $i \in X_{r}$. By Lemma~\ref{MatrixSum3.HasTuBr.cccAr_isTotallyUnimodular}.\ref{item:tss_Brp_c01}, $\begin{bmatrix} c_{0}'' (i) & c_{1}'' (i) \end{bmatrix} \in \{0, \pm 1\}^{\{y_{0}, y_{1}\}} \setminus \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \right\}$. Consider two cases.
nodes.statement_short: Sign patterns of c_0'', c_1'' from Lemma 31.

nodes.name: Case 1
nodes.statement: If $D_{0}'' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, then by item~\ref{item:tss_Bp_Deq} we have $D'' (i, Y_{\ell}) = c_{0}'' (i) \cdot d_{0}'' + (-c_{1}'' (i)) \cdot d_{1}''$. By considering all possible cases for $c_{0}'' (i)$ and $c_{1}'' (i)$, we conclude that $D'' (i, Y_{\ell}) \in \{0, \pm d_{0}'', \pm d_{1}'', \pm d_{2}''\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Case D_0'' = diag(1,-1).

nodes.name: Case 2
nodes.statement: If $D_{0}'' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, then by item~\ref{item:tss_Bp_Deq} we have $D'' (i, Y_{\ell}) = c_{0}'' (i) \cdot d_{0}'' + (c_{1}'' (i) - c_{0}'' (i)) \cdot d_{1}''$. By considering all possible cases for $c_{0}'' (i)$ and $c_{1}'' (i)$, we conclude that $D'' (i, Y_{\ell}) \in \{0, \pm d_{0}'', \pm d_{1}'', \pm d_{2}''\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Case D_0'' unitriangular.

nodes.name: Item 5
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{MatrixSum3.HasTuBr.dddAl_isTotallyUnimodular}.\ref{item:tss_Blp_tu3}, $\begin{bmatrix} A_{\ell}'' \\ d_{0}'' \\ d_{1}'' \\ d_{2}'' \end{bmatrix}$ is TU. Since TUness is preserved under adjoining zero rows, copies of existing rows, and multiplying rows by $\pm 1$ factors, $\begin{bmatrix} A_{\ell}'' \\ 0 \\ \pm d_{0}'' \\ \pm d_{1}'' \\ \pm d_{2}'' \end{bmatrix}$ is also TU. By item~\ref{item:tss_Bp_Drows}, $\begin{bmatrix} A_{\ell}'' \\ D'' \end{bmatrix}$ is a submatrix of the latter matrix, hence it is also TU.
nodes.statement_short: Item 5: [A_l''; D''] is a submatrix of a TU matrix built from rows ±d_i''.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Our goal is to show that $C'$ satisfies all properties from Definition~\ref{MatrixLikeSum3}. Let $C' = \begin{bmatrix} C_{11}' & C_{12}' \\ C_{21}' & C_{22}' \end{bmatrix}$, and let $\begin{bmatrix} A_{\ell}' \\ D' \end{bmatrix}$ be the result of performing a short tableau pivot on $(x, y)$ in $\begin{bmatrix} A_{\ell} \\ D \end{bmatrix}$. Observe the following.
nodes.statement_short: Name blocks of C' and of the pivoted left part.

nodes.name: Blocks of C'
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{Matrix.shortTableauPivot_zero}, $C_{11}' = A_{\ell}'$, $C_{12}' = 0$, $C_{21}' = D'$, and $C_{22}' = A_{r}$.
nodes.statement_short: Block structure of C' from the zero-block pivot lemma.

nodes.name: Entries of A_l
nodes.statement: Since $\begin{bmatrix} A_{\ell} \\ D \end{bmatrix}$ is TU by property~\ref{item:mls3_LeftTU} for $C$, all entries of $A_{\ell}$ are in $\{0, \pm 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Entries of A_l are 0/±1.

nodes.name: Pivot is unit
nodes.statement: $A_{\ell} (x, y) \in \{\pm 1\}$, as $A_{\ell} (x, y) \in \{0, \pm 1\}$ by the above observation and $A_{\ell} (x, y) \neq 0$ by the assumption.
nodes.statement_short: The pivot is ±1.

nodes.name: Left part TU
nodes.statement: Since $\begin{bmatrix} A_{\ell} \\ D \end{bmatrix}$ is TU by property~\ref{item:mls3_LeftTU} for $C$, and since pivoting preserves TUness, $\begin{bmatrix} A_{\ell}' \\ D' \end{bmatrix}$ is also TU.
nodes.statement_short: Pivoting keeps the left part TU.

nodes.name: Two properties
nodes.statement: These observations immediately imply properties~\ref{item:mls3_BottomTU} and~\ref{item:mls3_LeftTU} for $C'$. Indeed, property~\ref{item:mls3_BottomTU} holds for $C'$, since $C_{22}' = A_{r}$ and $\begin{bmatrix} c_{0} & c_{1} & c_{0} - c_{1} & A_{r} \end{bmatrix}$ is TU by property~\ref{item:mls3_BottomTU} for $C$. On the other hand, property~\ref{item:mls3_LeftTU} follows from $C_{11}' = A_{\ell}'$, $C_{21}' = D'$, and $\begin{bmatrix} A_{\ell}' \\ D' \end{bmatrix}$ being TU.
nodes.statement_short: Properties of bottom TU and left TU hold for C'.

nodes.name: Remaining property
nodes.statement: Thus, it only remains to show that $C'$ satisfies property~\ref{item:mls3_Parallels}. Let $j \in Y_{r}$. Our goal is to prove that $D' (X_{r}', j) \in \{0, \pm c_{0}, \pm c_{1}, \pm (c_{0} - c_{1})\}$.
nodes.statement_short: It remains to check the parallel-columns property.

nodes.name: Pivot column
nodes.statement: Suppose $j = y$. By the pivot formula, $D' (X_{r}', y) = -\frac{D (X_{r}', y)}{A_{\ell} (x, y)}$. Since $D (X_{r}', y) \in \{0, \pm c_{0}, \pm c_{1}, \pm (c_{0} - c_{1})\}$ by property~\ref{item:mls3_Parallels} for $C$ and since $A_{\ell} (x, y) \in \{\pm 1\}$, we get $D' (X_{r}', y) \in \{0, \pm c_{0}, \pm c_{1}, \pm (c_{0} - c_{1})\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pivot column: scaled by ±1.

nodes.name: Other columns
nodes.statement: Now suppose $j \in Y_{\ell} \setminus \{y\}$. By the pivot formula, $D' (X_{r}', j) = D (X_{r}', j) - \frac{A_{\ell} (x, j)}{A_{\ell} (x, y)} \cdot D (X_{r}', y)$. Here $D (X_{r}', j), \ D (X_{r}', y) \in \{0, \pm c_{0}, \pm c_{1}, \pm (c_{0} - c_{1})\}$ by property~\ref{item:mls3_Parallels} for $C$, and $A_{\ell} (x, j) \in \{0, \pm 1\}$ and $A_{\ell} (x, y) \in \{\pm 1\}$ by the prior observations. Perform an exhaustive case distinction on $D (X_{r}', j)$, $D (X_{r}', y)$, $A_{\ell} (x, j)$, and $A_{\ell} (x, y)$. The number of cases can be significantly reduced by using symmetries. In every remaining case, we can either show that $D' (X_{r}', j) \in \{0, \pm c_{0}, \pm c_{1}, \pm (c_{0} - c_{1})\}$, as desired, or obtain a contradiction with property~\ref{item:mls3_AuxTU}.
nodes.statement_short: Other columns: exhaustive case analysis using symmetries and the auxiliary TU property.

nodes.name: Reduce to k-PU
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{Matrix.isTotallyUnimodular_iff_forall_isPartiallyUnimodular}, it suffices to show that $C$ is $k$-PU for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$. We prove this claim by induction on $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce TU to k-PU for all k; induct on k.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: The base case with $k = 1$ holds, since properties~\ref{item:mls3_BottomTU} and~\ref{item:mls3_LeftTU} in Definition~\ref{MatrixLikeSum3} imply that $A_{\ell}$, $A_{r}$, and $D$ are TU, so all their entries of $C = \begin{bmatrix} A_{\ell} & 0 \\ D & A_{r} \end{bmatrix}$ are in $\{0, \pm 1\}$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Base case: entries are 0/±1.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Suppose that for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$ we know that every $C' \in \mathcal{C} (X_{\ell}', Y_{\ell}', X_{r}', Y_{r}'; c_{0}, c_{1})$ is $k$-PU. Our goal is to show that $C$ is $(k + 1)$-PU, i.e., that every $(k + 1) \times (k + 1)$ submatrix $S$ of $C$ has $\det V \in \{0, \pm 1\}$. First, suppose that $V$ has no rows in $X_{\ell}'$. Then $V$ is a submatrix of $\begin{bmatrix} D & A_{r} \end{bmatrix}$, which is TU by property~\ref{item:mls3_BottomTU} in Definition~\ref{MatrixLikeSum3}, so $\det V \in \{0, \pm 1\}$. Thus, we may assume that $S$ contains a row $x_{\ell} \in X_{\ell}'$. Next, note that without loss of generality we may assume that there exists $y_{\ell} \in Y_{\ell}'$ such that $V (x_{\ell}, y_{\ell}) \neq 0$. Indeed, if $V (x_{\ell}, y) = 0$ for all $y$, then $\det V = 0$ and we are done, and $V (x_{\ell}, y) = 0$ holds whenever $y \in Y_{r}'$. Since $C$ is $1$-PU, all entries of $V$ are in $\{0, \pm 1\}$, and hence $V (x_{\ell}, y_{\ell}) \in \{\pm 1\}$. Thus, by Lemma~\ref{shortTableauPivot_submatrix_det_abs_eq_div}, performing a short tableau pivot in $V$ on $(x_{\ell}, y_{\ell})$ yields a matrix that contains a $k \times k$ submatrix $S''$ such that $|\det V| = |\det V''|$. Since $V$ is a submatrix of $C$, matrix $V''$ is a submatrix of the matrix $C'$ resulting from performing a short tableau pivot in $C$ on the same entry $(x_{\ell}, y_{\ell})$. By Lemma~\ref{MatrixLikeSum3.shortTableauPivot}, we have $C' \in \mathcal{C} (X_{\ell}', Y_{\ell}', X_{r}', Y_{r}'; c_{0}, c_{1})$. Thus, by the inductive hypothesis applied to $V''$ and $C'$, we have $\det V'' \in \{0, \pm 1\}$. Since $|\det V| = |\det V''|$, we conclude that $\det V \in \{0, \pm 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step via pivoting within the family C.
